planting.note: Plant tuberous roots in spring in rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; parrot lily has naturalized widely across the Gulf South and can spread aggressively by underground stolons once established.

directions: Plant tuberous roots about six inches deep in rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun, handling the brittle roots carefully. Parrot lily bears striking, dark red flowers streaked and tipped in deep maroon-green, distinctive markings that give the plant its common name, blooming on wiry stems from spring into summer. Unlike many Peruvian lily hybrids, this species has naturalized extensively across the Gulf South, spreading by underground stolons to form substantial colonies in shaded gardens, old homesites, and woodland edges, so give it room or plan to periodically thin it where a contained planting is wanted. It goes dormant in the heat of summer and resprouts with cooler fall weather in many gardens, and established colonies are extremely drought-tolerant and low-maintenance once settled in.

common_name: Indian Summer Alstroemeria (Bronze-Foliaged Orange-Flowered Peruvian Lily)

planting.note: Plant tuberous roots in spring about six inches deep in rich, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Indian Summer pairs dark bronze-purple foliage with vivid orange, red-flecked flowers.

directions: Plant tuberous roots about six inches deep in rich, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, handling the brittle roots carefully. Indian Summer pairs dark, chocolate-bronze foliage with vivid, warm orange flowers flecked and streaked with deep red, a striking color combination that sets it apart from most Peruvian lily hybrids, which typically have plain green leaves. It blooms over a long season from late spring into fall, and pulling rather than cutting spent flower stems from the base stimulates continued rebloom by removing the seed-forming stem entirely. In colder zones mulch heavily for winter protection or lift the roots for storage, and divide congested clumps every few years in spring if flowering declines.

common_name: Rock and Roll Alstroemeria (Variegated Cream-and-Green with Pink Flowers)

planting.note: Plant tuberous roots in spring about six inches deep in rich, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Rock and Roll bears cream-and-green variegated foliage that provides ornamental value even before the plant flowers.

directions: Plant tuberous roots about six inches deep in rich, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, handling the brittle roots carefully. Rock and Roll bears attractive cream-and-green variegated foliage that provides ornamental interest even when the plant is not in bloom, topped by clear pink, orchid-like flowers with darker pink and yellow streaking through the growing season. Its variegated leaves make it a good textural companion in a mixed container or border even before flowering begins. Pulling rather than cutting spent flower stems from the base stimulates continued rebloom. In colder zones mulch heavily for winter protection or lift the roots for storage, and divide congested clumps every few years in spring if flowering declines.

common_name: Inca Ice Alstroemeria (Cream-White with Yellow Throat)

planting.note: Plant tuberous roots in spring about six inches deep in rich, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Inca Ice bears pale cream-white flowers, a cooler tone than the warm oranges and reds typical of the genus.

directions: Plant tuberous roots about six inches deep in rich, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, handling the brittle roots carefully. Inca Ice bears pale, cool cream-white orchid-like flowers with a soft yellow throat and fine reddish-brown streaking, a gentler color than the warm oranges and reds typical of most Peruvian lily cultivars, making it a versatile choice for pastel or white-themed cutting gardens. The flowers are exceptionally long-lasting when cut, often holding for two weeks or more in a vase. Pulling rather than cutting spent flower stems from the base stimulates continued rebloom by removing the entire seed-forming stem. In colder zones mulch heavily for winter protection or lift the roots for storage.

common_name: Ligtu Hybrid Alstroemeria (Classic Mixed-Color Chilean Strain)

planting.note: Plant tuberous roots in spring about six inches deep in rich, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; Ligtu hybrids are a classic mixed-color strain derived from Chilean species, blooming in a broad range of pastel and warm tones.

directions: Plant tuberous roots about six inches deep in rich, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, handling the brittle roots carefully. Ligtu hybrids are a long-cultivated Chilean-derived seed strain producing orchid-like flowers across a wide range of colors including cream, pink, orange, salmon, and red, often with contrasting streaking on the upper petals, blooming heavily in late spring to early summer before going dormant in the heat. Because it is a mixed seed strain rather than a single named clone, individual plants vary somewhat in color, giving naturalized drifts extra variety. Pulling rather than cutting spent flower stems from the base stimulates continued rebloom during the flowering season. In colder zones mulch heavily for winter protection or lift the roots for storage.
